utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Judge Thelin is not able to sit today, and I think that will be the case tomorrow as well. But in the expectation that at least by Monday he will able to resume and continue sitting, the Chamber is taking -- has taken the view that this is a case in which it should continue today and tomorrow pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please stand, and would you read the affirmation on the card that is offered to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down, and Mr. Saxon will take over at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I begin with the witness, it is the Prosecution's sad duty to inform the Chamber that last night Mr. Mettraux was correct and the Prosecution was wrong regarding the paragraph 08 in the consolidated witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think that you need be sad that Mr. Mettraux is right. No doubt he is feeling satisfied, but these sorts of oversights can occur without the need for sadness, just a need for frank acceptance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. And the Prosecution will keep its upper lip stiff and move on. The Prosecution's suggest, and I believe Mr. Mettraux will agree, is that if the Trial Chamber determines that the consolidated witness statement of this witness should be admitted, that the record be noted that paragraph 08 should not form part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the necessary consequence given the present procedural orders; and as I think was indicated last evening, it will be for the -- your own decision whether in any oral questioning of the witness you wish to pursue that subject matter or not. So you better move on to identify the statement or move formally, or is that what you feel you have now done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have some questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, your name is Henry Bolton?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you are a citizen of the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in 2001 and 2002, you were employed by the international organisation known as the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, specifically, you were working in Macedonia at that time, right?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall that in August of 2003 and the first part of 2006, you gave witness statements to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I recall that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall more recently, just last month, those two witness statements were effectively consolidated, and you signed the so-called consolidated witness statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when did you that, after you did that, did you also make some addendums or additions or corrections to your consolidated witness statement?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were those additions or corrections recorded in another document dated the 18th of May, 2007?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall the exact date, but, yes, in May, mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when read together, would these two statements -- and did you the opportunity to review what you were signing in your own language, before you signed them?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And together would this consolidated witness statement and the addendum form what you would say before this Court this morning if you were to testify orally?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: They would provide an accurate account of the events, as I know them to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, at this time, I would move for the admission under Rule 92 ter of Mr. Bolton's consolidated witness statement and the addendum thereto. We have copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With the deletion of one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With the deletion of paragraph 08 in the consolidated witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement will become Exhibit 236.1, and the addendum will become Exhibit P236.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Witness Henry Bolton is a British citizen who served as head of the OSCE field office in Radishani, Macedonia in 2001. The area of responsibility of this field office included the village of Ljuboten. Mr. Bolton's current occupation is senior border issues advisor with the OSCE secretariat in Vienna. On the 10th of August, 2001, the witness heard an explosion from the direction of Ljuboten. Mr. Bolton attempted to enter Ljuboten to investigate, but was prevented from doing so. On 11 August 2001, the witness heard small arms fire, mortar fire, and explosions in the areas of Ljubotenski Bacila and Ljubanka Reka. On the 12th of August, 2001, the witness observed extensive small arms fire and mortar and grenade detonations in Ljuboten. The witness was unable to gain access to Ljuboten until 14 August 2001. On that day, the witness saw five bodies in Ljuboten, three of which were in a field to the north of the village. The bodies were dressed in civilian clothes and had numerous gunshot wounds. The witness observed damage to and destruction of property, including homes, farm machinery, and livestock. The witness speaks of the possible cause and manner of death of the dead persons and evidence of weaponry used during the attack. The witness states that he found no evidence of prepared physical defences in the village of Ljuboten or evidence of exchanges of fire in the areas where the bodies were found. The witness's evidence also addresses the following topics: The centralisation of authority and chain of command within the Macedonian Ministry of Interior; the Croatian operation and chain of command of special units of the Macedonian Ministry of Interior; police operations during the year 2001; and case management within the Ministry of Interior. Could we please show the witness what is -- before we do that, Your Honour, we have several binders containing copies of the documents which we will use with the witness this morning, if I could ask the usher's assistance to distribute them to you. And if I could ask the court officer's assistance to show the witness what is tab 1 in the Judge's binder. It's Rule 65 ter numbers 691.1 and 691.2. It has the ERN range in English N001-5590 through 5601. We can start with this page; that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, if you can perhaps help us, please, just for a moment, while you were working with the OSCE in the summer of 2001, did you become familiar with an organisation or agency known as the Crisis Management Centre?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was the Crisis Management Centre?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: The Crisis Management Centre Organised was a body, I believe, that was run or organised by the Ministry of Defence of Macedonia and provided for an interagency coordination and response to the crisis and provided for an interface between the Macedonian authorities involved with the crisis and the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in the course of your duties, as a member of the OSCE, did you have occasion to receive reports that were produced by the Crisis Centre?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move to what is probably two pages further on in this range, N001-5590, please. It's a little bit -- the problem is the diagram on the right-hand side. We're losing -- we're missing a bit of the right side of the diagram, but let's start with this for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see in the centre, this particular diagram is entitled "Organisational Set-up of the Centre." We see the president at the top, the Security Council below that, principle coordination committee below that, and then we see the Crisis Management Centre. Do you see what I'm speaking about on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To the right, do you notice there is a box, and it says "Minister of Interior." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It's not very clear, but, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And below that there are three letters, CGS, and then arrows pointing to the Crisis Management Centre. Do you know what the acronym "CGS" stood for?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: In this particular case, I'm not certain, but I understand generally that that acronym stands for Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before the line that says "Crisis Management Centre," there's the word "Plans," and then below that, we see two acronyms. One says "MOI," and the other says "MOD." At that time, what did the letters MOI stand for, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the letters MOD?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we look a bit over on the right-hand side of the diagram, there is a word in black that says "Coordination," and below that the letters "IC" with a slash "Allies." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Below that we see several abbreviations: EUMM; we see OSCE; K4; NCCC; et cetera. Can you explain why these organisations were listed here?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: There was a coordination mechanism between the international agencies present in Macedonia at that time, and this is list of those organisations and bodies, including it goes on to bilateral; that is, interested bilateral diplomatic missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was information regularly shared during the crisis between organisations such as the OSCE and the Crisis Management Centre?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page of this ERN range, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This appears to be a cover letter coming from the Republic of Macedonia Crisis Management Centre. It's dated Skopje, July 27, 2001, and the subject is "Summary of the events in the crisis areas in the Republic of Macedonia since the establishment of cease-fire, July 5th, 2001." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you personally recall this particular document?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: As I see it there, that was a standard cover document for a report that was written on a daily basis. But that particular one, as it stands there, is the same as all the others that we produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page, please, 5592. It is another document. Well, that appears to be an error. No, but this is part of the same document, actually. It's all -- it's why it is part of the same ERN range.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could take a look at the document, the page that is in front of you right now, again, it's from the Crisis Management Centre, situation in the crisis areas after the cease-fire of July 5, 2001. Can you tell us what was the cease-fire that was enacted on the 5th of July, generally?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yeah. This was the agreement brokered by the international community to seize hostilities between what we were referring to as ethnic Albanian armed groups and the Macedonian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You used the term "ethnic Albanian armed groups." Who were you actually referring to when you use this term?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It's safe to say that we were talking about the NLA, the National Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And tis term "ethnic Albanian armed groups," why did you and your organisation decide to use this term?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: This was a decision that was, I think, made by the internationally community generally, and was a generic term to cover all Albanian armed groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was there a particular problem perhaps of referring to the NLA in your reports, a particular problem with their acronym?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: There was a problem in that the translation into Macedonian actually became the same as the acronym for the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. And so was the term "ethnic Albanian armed groups" a method of avoiding confusing these two groups?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see below there is a line there, it says, "Inhabited places in which the terrorists exercised control on the day of the cease-fire." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then there is a list of villages below that. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, we see a line saying, "Inhabited places besides the aforementioned in which the terrorists exercised control after the cease-fire," and then we see a number of place names below that. Further on down the page, there is a heading. It says, "Definition of Terms." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says: "Exercising control means establishing alternative structures of authority by the terrorists through restraining freedom of movement and maltreatment of citizens by establishing check-points, establishing authority bodies in the so-called liberated territories." Mr. Bolton, help us with this. While you were working with the OSCE in 2001, did the OSCE ever calculate the number of villages that were controlled, so to speak, by the NLA?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Not only the OSCE, this was done in conjunction with other international organisations as well, and the Macedonian authorities. And we came to a figure which I believe was 138. It was somewhere between 135 and 140.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that number refers to different villages?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Different villages, and we applied the principle that the police did not have access or were able to carry out their duties in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say you "applied that principle," was that was the definition that you and other members of the international community used in terms of defining where the NLA exercised control?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Below that paragraph, we see a line saying "General features of the conditions after this are as follows," and then a number of subjects are mentioned, and talking about sporadic shooting, attacks against the security forces of Macedonia, free redeployment of the armed groups from one location to another, reinforcement of the defence positions by strengthening the fortifications, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the next page, move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you look at subheading 2 at the top of the next page, I'll wait for the Macedonian version to come up on the screen. There it is. Subheading 2 there lists "Exercising control by establishing alternative authority structures by the terrorists," and below that we see: "Restraining treatment of movement, maltreatment of citizens by establishes check-points, establishing authority bodies in the so-called liberated areas, improved self-confidence of the terrorists, which suggests the wish to establish alternative mechanisms of law an order." While you were working in Macedonia, during the crisis in 2001, did you observe these different dynamics that are listed here?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a chart produced by the Crisis Centre, titled, "Non-compliance with the cease-fire in the crisis areas." There's a total at the bottom, a total of 788 separate violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could then move to what is ERN 5599, three or four pages further along, and if we could perhaps focus on the bottom of this page, please. Part of the same report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see there there's a subheading titled "Tetovo Crisis Area." Why was Tetovo considered part of the crisis area? What was going on there?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Tetovo had been a centre of difficulties, exchanges of fire, abductions, and so on. It was one of the most intense areas of the overall crisis area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were there parts of Tetovo that were effectively controlled, to use the definition of your organisation, by the NLA?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: If I can divide it slightly. There is the town ever Tetovo itself which, was mostly controlled by the Macedonians; but the outlying areas, particularly to the south, the west, and the north of Tetovo, were controlled by the NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move, please, to N001-5601, which is two pages further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And here on this page -- I'm waiting for the Macedonian version to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have been advised that for some reason the Macedonian original version of this page is not available. The Defence counsel have hard copies of both the English and Macedonian version, I believe, but I may stand to be corrected. I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We only have the English version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Will the Chamber allow me to proceed, Your Honour, with a couple of questions about this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, but I trust that you will remedy the deficiency, ensuring that is available to the Defence in the other language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On this page heading 2, it says, "Skopje Crisis Area," and why was Skopje considered a crisis area?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Skopje was included in the overall crisis areas because it was an area in which there were also a number of incidents, at that time, less than Tetovo, but it was still an area in which the NLA were active. And if I may add, the same applies, that it was the more rural areas in which the NLA were more active, rather than, if you like, the city of Skopje itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And below that it refers to the "Kumanovo Crisis Area." Why was Kumanovo considered to be a crisis area?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: For the same reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the same reason.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I might add that the division, in this sense, reflects the structure of the Macedonian security forces at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand that last comment.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: The division into three areas of this sort, Tetovo, Skopje and Kumanovo, reflected the regional police headquarters covering those areas. These were geographical areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would tender what is the ERN range N001-5588 through N001-5601.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just two short things. In relation to the first document, Your Honour, that is the chart of the Security Council, coordination committee. I was wondering whether my colleague from the Prosecution will explore with the witness whether he can give any evidence about the authenticity and the origin of the document, because we have no information about this. And the second matter, Your Honour, about the second document with which the Prosecution has used. We do understand that the Prosecution does not wish to tender that document for the truth of its content. It hasn't actually put the proposition from the document to Mr. Bolton. Mr. Bolton has given very clear evidence about the matter, as he could give evidence about, and I am just evidence wondering what the purpose is for the Prosecution to give seek the document, whether it is simply to corroborate the evidence of Mr. Bolton, or whether it is to rely on the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution does seek to rely on the contents of the document. That is the first point. And the Prosecution believes that the responses of Mr. Bolton have not only explained but also verified the accuracy of several portions of this document. This document was received by -- from the Prosecution, from the OSCE which was the institution where Mr. Bolton worked. I can ask, if it would be helpful, one more question, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful both to the Chamber and to the Defence, Mr. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, how often would the Crisis Management Centre produce reports?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Initially, as I arrived, it was slightly intermittent, as I recall. Later on, it became a daily event. About this time, it was a daily event; and then later on, as the crisis subsided, the reports became less frequent, as did the meetings between the international community and the Crisis Management Centre staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And while you were working in Macedonia, during the summer of 2001, did you receive copies of materials produced by the Crisis Management Centre, like this?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did. More often than not, they were controlled and I had visibility of them, but not necessarily received them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And does this document that we have reviewed this morning, does this resemble the materials that you received -- that you viewed at that time as coming from the Crisis Management Centre?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is there anything about it that looks like it was not produced by the Crisis Management Centre.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first document, I'm not sure whether the answers were meant to relate to that or not, the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn to what is tab 1 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would these kind of charts, would you see -- would you see or receive charts such as this in your capacity as an employee of the OSCE at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot state that this particular chart is one that I saw, but it is -- it is extremely familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything further, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Nothing further. We would persist and I think if the Prosecution seeks to rely on the accuracy of the truth of the document contained in particular in relation to the chart, I think, at least, a question could be put, in fairness to Mr. Bolton, whether he agrees with the presentation and the structure in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just to speed things up, Mr. Bolton, does the content of the chart agree with your understanding of the functioning of the structure that is set out there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It does. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told, Mr. Saxon, that this document, in the form you're tendering it, has not been made available in e-court. You are, in fact, quoting pages from three distinct documents, but not the complete part of the those three distinct documents. I think that is simply a matter of coordination between your technical support and the e-court people, but it would be more simple if this document could be provided in appropriate form, and what I propose to do is to hold the formal admission of the document, as you tender it, in the hope that you will be able to help with the technical problem being presented at the moment. The motion will be granted if and when we can get some resolution of those technical issues, so that could be done during the break or at some convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps it just might assist Your Honour. It was the Prosecution's understanding that these materials, this ERN range that we have reviewed with Mr. Bolton, were uploaded in e-court as 691.1 and 691.2, and that was simply our understanding. Am I misspeaking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The indication I am being given is that that is not a correct understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then we will do our best to clarify the situation soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Proceed on the basis that the documents, as in the tab, will be received as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could turn to the second tab in Your Honours' binder, and this is actually what the Prosecution believes is in e-court as 691.4, and it is a document bearing ERN N001-5670 to -- May I have the Court's indulgence for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. This would be document beginning with N001-5670, please. The description in Your Honours -- the description for this tab, I note, is incorrect. The description should say, "An OSCE report dated the 15th of July, 2001, drafted by Henry Bolton." In the Macedonian version, can we go back to 5670, please. Your Honour, again, I'm told that there is a page not available on e-court in the Macedonian version, which the Prosecution will remedy as soon as it possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, can you please look at the English page that is in front of you. It has the number 70 up at the top, and you see it has your name on it?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this fax is addressed to the "Crisis Management Centre, Major Jone Ivanovski," and it is a cease-fire monitoring report from the 14th of July to the 15th of July. And down below we see a signature over your name. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It is my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know this gentleman, Major Ivanovski, who is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I know that I spoke to him on the telephone on a number of occasions. I can't recall whether I ever met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know what institution he worked for?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can you briefly describe what were your duties when you first arrived in Macedonia, please?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: When I was first arrived, I was allocated to Team Centre, which was the Skopje team; however, for a brief period of time, I did work in the -- the OSCE coordination cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was the OSCE coordination centre?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: This was, you might call it, the operations room for the mission, which we ran jointly with the European Monitoring Mission. It was the point to which the reports from the field of cease-fire violations came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when reports from the field came in, what was done with that information in the coordination centre?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: They were collated at the end of each reporting period, each 24 hours, into a consolidated list of incidents and events, which resulted in a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why would you send such reports to the Crisis Management Centre?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Because we had a presence in the field, and we got an agreement that we would share our reporting with the Crisis Management Centre. We were also the point of contact in the mission for the Crisis Management Centre, when there was an incident, that they might report to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say "we had an agreement," who is we?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: We, the international community. I was not present in Macedonia at the time that the agreement was set up, but I understood that this mechanism was in place by the agreement of, if you like, the both sides; the Macedonian authorities and ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please, which is has the title, "Cease-fire Monitoring Log," 14th of July to 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can recall, is this how your reports were produced?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you see in the second item -- I'll wait for the Macedonian version. Here it is. The second item contains information from the OSCE team A-2. Information was sent at 1725, and it's about a check-point being established, and the information says this: "The ethnic Albanian armed group established openly a check-point in Trnovace; 15 uniformed men armed with Kalashnikov type weapons and one grenade launcher; a large sign 'UCK stop' had been erected; the situation was reported as team A-2 as tense and unfriendly." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question is this, if you're following me?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The establishment of such check-points, how common was in that in the summer of 2001?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That was common.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you have personal experience, for example, either seeing or trying to move through --

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- such check-points?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can, Your Honour, at this point, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P237, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if Your Honours would turn to what is tab 3 in your binder, and what I'd like to discuss with the witness now are some excerpts from an exhibit already admitted, P0045. It's a long document called "The White Book, Terrorism of the So-called NLA." And if we can first see ERN N005-7608, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, this is the cover page of this publication, published by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, please, 7610, or perhaps two pages further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see it's given the date at the bottom, Skopje 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could now move, please, to ERN N005-7651, which is page 46 of this document. I'm just waiting for the Macedonian page to come up.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Without a reference number in the Macedonian, we are unable to find it, to find the exact page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Reference number in Macedonian. Can we move to page 46 of the Macedonian version, please, and can we move back, please. In other words, can we move -- is it possible to move back page by page, until we see the subheading "8669, 15 March 2000"? Your Honours, I will move on. I will move on at this time. I don't want to take more time of the Court. I will just ask a question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness, when you were working in Macedonia in 2001, what was the proportion of ethnic Albanians in the Macedonian police forces that you observed?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I can't say precisely, but it was low.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "low," can you give your own estimate of a ratio?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Probably somewhere in around 1 in 80 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One police officer out of 80 might be an ethnic Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Mm-hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Are you able to recall an incident on the 10th of -- on the 8th of August, 2001, involving an ambush on a Macedonian army convoy?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did that happen on the highway between Skopje and Tetovo?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you tell us please how you first heard about this incident?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I had a report. I was contacted, I can't honestly remember how, but I would expect it have been through our -- our coordination centre, that there had been shooting on the highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I went -- I was on the western side of Skopje anyway, and I moved towards the start of the highway where there is a police check-point. I was initially stopped at that check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, eventually, were you allowed to pass through the check-point?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I proceeded down the highway until such a point as I came across the back of an army convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you see?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: In terms of the convoy, I saw a number of vehicles, both armoured vehicles, but predominantly soft-skinned trucks, static, nosed-tail. And in front much them, there was a burning soft-skinned truck. There were a number of bodies across the road and unexploded ordnance across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And by "bodies," you mean dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: At that time, I presumed they were dead and, in fact, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: An officer came jogging up to me and said that the convoy had to move on, jumped back in a vehicle, and, indeed, military vehicles present did move on in the direction of Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you do at that time?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I stayed there to assess what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I stop you there.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have a military background?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe it for us, please?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: For 11 years, I was in the regular army, subsequently in the territorial army or reserve army. I held the rank of acting major. I served, operationally, in a number of parts of the world. I saw active service in Central America.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you, during those 11 years, become familiar with different types of weapons, ordnance, munitions, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did. In fact, I am more familiar than, that is often the case, as a qualified range manager and instructor in infantry weapons of all sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So after the members of this convoy, who had survived, drove off, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, my responsibility at the time was to report on incidents, so I wanted to record details of the scene. I also had to report back to our coordination centre and the Crisis Management Centre as to what the situation was. Due to difficulties in communication, I was instructed to report directly to the Crisis Management Centre by our coordination centre, the OSCE coordination centre, and this I did. And that was my initial -- do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did other persons arrive along that highway?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who arrived?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: As we were doing this, first of all, a large truck came down the highway. At that point, I should say the highway is -- now has a central reservation. At that time, the highway was still partially under construction, and only the southern highway was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: A large truck came from the direction of Tetovo towards the incident --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: -- and towards the unexploded ordnance, which included mortar bombs lying on the road. I stopped that truck, and behind that truck were large number of other civilian vehicles; Cars, buses, and so on, and other trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were those other vehicles also stopped?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: They were. And what happened after these vehicles travelling along the road stopped?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Initially, everything was calm; but after a few minutes, 15 minutes or so, they started to realise, I think, that they were in a potentially danger situation and wanted to move on, something that I understand. I was reluctant to let them do so, however, driving over an unexploded ordnance and bodies. There was a lot of shouting and emotion going on. I moved to the side of the road where there is a concrete revetment, to sort of clear my head and think about what to do next. As I looked down, I saw two electrical wires coming down from the area that I had assumed to be the firing position of the ambush that had taken place. I walked along the revetment, looking at these wires and saw they went into a culvert, a drainage tunnel, if you look, under the road, directly underneath the civilian traffic. With my military background and our experiences in Northern Ireland, which although I haven't been to Northern Ireland I'm very well aware of the types of techniques there, I immediately suspected, what we call, a culvert bomb, a bomb in such a drainage tunnel that is placed to cause maximum damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A bomb placed underneath a road?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Suspecting this, and with the knowledge of explosives and tactics used in such cases, I could not guarantee that that bomb would not go off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I stop you there?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you find explosives?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: More or less how much?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't actually crawl into the -- in the tunnel itself, and couldn't tell you how much from my direct observation; but I understand later, from contacts within the Ministry of Interior of Macedonia, that it was around 300 to 350 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So when you saw these explosives that were placed underneath the road, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I immediately understood the danger to the civilian traffic, removed some of the ordnance, and moved the -- or directed the traffic across the highway to the still under construction part, the part that was still being built and was not open to traffic normally, but where there were also some bodies, one of which we had to move slightly to allow the traffic through. That -- so the objective being to get civilian traffic out of the area as quickly as possible to avoid any casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you saw you "moved some of the ordnance," your referring to ordnance that was littering the surface of the road?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after that, was that event ever discussed on Macedonian television?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It was. The public prosecutor later thanked the OSCE team for saving life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn to what is tab 4 in Your Honours's binder. This Rule 65 ter number 267. It begins with N000-0002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bolton, if you take a look at the English version here, you see this is an OSCE report, and it says, "From Henry Bolton, Team Centre; to Ambassador Carlo Ungaro. " And who was Ambassador Ungaro?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: He was the OSCE head of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is in the summer of 2001?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is dated 15th of August, 2001, and it is cc'd to persons: Robin Seward, Morris Kanavan, Andrew Venis, and Eileen Simpson. "Subject: The five bodies observed in the village of Ljuboten." Do you recall writing this report?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when did you go to the village of Ljuboten, after the events of the 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: When did I go?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: On the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, very briefly, what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Firstly, made contact with villagers to find out what -- the initial account of what had been occurring in the village in the days preceding our visit there, preceding the 14th; and then having understood from them that there were bodies in the village, went to investigate that scene or to look at that scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, do you also have a police background?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yeah. Following leaving the regular army in 1990, I joined the British police. I undertook a number of roles within the British police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kind of training do you have, training and/or experience, in crime scene investigation forensics, things like that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: All British police are trained in crime scene preservation and in gathering of evidence, both physical material evidence and witness evidence. In terms of specialist forensics training, I have none; although, I have worked closely with scenes of crime officers whilst they have been collecting evidence in cases that I have been involved with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say you "have worked close with scenes of crimes officers," on investigations, where would you have done that, what countries?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That was in the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And have you also worked on investigations of crime, violent crime in parts of the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I would say that my role has been predominantly monitoring events. I worked alongside the Serbian police very closely in 1998 and 1999 in Kosovo, and was also involved in investigating an incident that happened in the village of Rogovo, on behalf of international authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where in Kosovo where you working?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: In the south, I was based in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in the Prizren area, were you often called out to examine scenes of violent crime?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Regularly?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you view a lot of gunshot wounds?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can take a look at the second page of your report, please, the next page. If we can focus on the third full paragraph which, again, with the words: "Along the length of the road." Do you see that paragraph, Mr. Bolton?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the beginning of paragraph, you explain or you wrote that "There was a large quantity (hundreds) of spent 7.62 short and long bullet cases, as well as numerous cardboard ammunition cartons," and then it says, "Other items observed were three M-80 64-millimetre RBR launcher tubes," and you explain that an RBR is a Russian manufactured shoulder-launched light anti-tank rocket that cannot be reloaded. Were you familiar with these kinds of weapons in your experience?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I was. When I say RBR is a Russian manufactured weapon, it is -- it's fundamentally a Russian design. I am familiar that weapon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then in the following paragraph, you refer to the body of Sulejman Bajrami, and then nearby, you refer to the body of Muharem Ramadani; and then you refer to bodies in a field, the bodies of Kadri Jashari, Bajram Jashari, and then someone who was only referred to as Bajrami. Why was one person only referred to by one name in your report?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Because that was the only name that I was given by local villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we move to the next page, please. There is a paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph. It says: "At the time of observation, all five bodies appeared to be wearing the same clothes that they had been wearing at the time of death." Do you see that, Mr. Bolton?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "The reason for this belief is the fact that the clothes were stained with what appeared to be blood and damage to the clothing corresponded with damage to the bodies."

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this was your assessment at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says: "In all five cases, the clothing worn by the bodies was of a civilian nature. No camouflage or uniformed items were observed, and no insignia or military equipment was seen." Two bullet points below that, there is a line and it says this: "There were no defensive positions observed in the village." Can you help us, please. What did you mean by "defensive positions"?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I mean, any sort of position that was -- that appeared to be prepared, to provide a secure point from which to fire at anyone. A prepared position for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, for example, at that time, during the crisis time in 2001 in Macedonia, what kind of defensive positions, prepared positions might you see in a particular conflicted area?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: You might see basements, which commonly in that area have small windows at ground level. You might see those blocked with sandbags. You might see rough walls to provide cover between buildings. You might see trenches built. These are all things that occurred elsewhere in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You didn't see any of this in the village of Ljuboten on the 14th of August?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Below, at the end of the report, we see a sentence: "There was no evidence of the ethnic Albanian armed group having used weapons fired from within the village." What kind of evidence might have indicated that the NLA had fired weapons within the village? What were you looking for?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Discarded, used cases, the brass case that holds the explosive that products the bullet from the weapon, when it is ejected from the weapon, it falls on the ground. You would expect, in such a case, if there was fire, you would expect to see those cases, and you expect to see them in positions that provided cover for the firer, generally, in a -- certainly in an extended fire-fight. People would take cover, and you see these behind the point of cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But you did say you found some spent ammunition cases?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, many hundreds. These were -- from looking at the overall scene, there was discarded ammunition and cardboard ammunition cartons, as I say. These were, although scattered over a wide area, predominantly behind points or at points that would provide the firer from cover from potential fire from the -- from the east, at which indicated to me that the firers had progressed up the road from the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: There were no empty cases on the eastern side of cover --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: -- which is what I would expect if there had been an exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document, please, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P238, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to try to finish up in the next ten minutes. If we can take a look at what is tab 5 in Your Honours's materials, and this is a photo from 65 ter 201, photo number 95 or the 95th photo. It has ERN N000-2184.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Bolton, did you take photographs in Ljuboten on the 14th of August?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: To record the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can look, please, at the photograph in front of you, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does it depicts?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It depicts the body of a male on the right-hand side of the road, as you look at, it lying face down. It depicts what I believe to be blood on the asphalt surface of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was this the first body that you encountered when you were in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P239, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can look at photograph with ERN number N000-2490, also from 65 ter 201, the sixth photograph. We're looking for N000-2094, one photograph before this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what does it depict?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It depicts the same body of a male as in the previous photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did you notice or what did you observe about this body?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That it had a number of injuries. The injuries on the right forearm are obvious in the photograph. In addition, there was an injury to the back of the neck or back of the head. The front of the head, which you can't see clearly in this photograph, was blown out. There were also injuries to the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you form an opinion as to what had caused these injuries?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: A gunshot wounds, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P240, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could move to what is tab 7, another photograph from 65 ter 2001. It is the 47th photograph, N000-2316.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in this photograph, we see that the shirt on this body has been pulled up along the back. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: To photograph the injuries to the back more, more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P241, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could look briefly at Exhibit P185, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, did you take this photograph on the 14th of August?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what were you trying to show in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I was trying to show two things: One is the fact that the front of the head had been -- had suffered extreme injury, and the second was the correlation to that to the injury on the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could now turn to exhibit number P186, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was this the second body that you observed on the 14th of August?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what kind of injuries did you observe on this body?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: The injury to the chest that is -- that's shown in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you form an opinion as to what caused the injury?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that that is the exit wound of a high velocity bullet. There were two, what I believe to be, entry wounds in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn now, please, to what is tab 10, and it is another photograph from 65 ter 201, the 22nd photograph. It has ERN number N000-2111.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we also see on the photograph it appears to have been annotated. We see a rectangular with the letters BJ, one with BY, one with KJ. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who put those letters there?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did you did know that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: For my own notes, if you like, as to which body was in which position. Those circles above the rectangles represent the positions of three bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there is one rectangle that has the initials BY. Can you tell us why the initials BY were placed there?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I can. Because that is the body that relates to the person we mentioned earlier, Bajrami, and that is the only name I had for that person. BY, in English, represents "by," which leads me to Bajrami. The other way of spelling it would be "BJ," which we already had a BJ, and I wasn't the to avoid confusion. It was just a way for me to differentiate between the three, or those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. We see a house to the left of the areas where the bodies were.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall anything in particular about the condition of that house at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yeah. That house had been you severely damaged by fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P242, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention that the transcript records at line 25 of 36 an extended answer of the witness, but attributed to Judge Van den Wyngaert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect to Your Honour Judge Van den Wyngaert, I believe the record should be corrected to reflect that it came from Mr. Bolton. If we could turn to what is the photograph in tab 11, which comes from 65 ter 201, the 17th photograph. It has As ERN N000-2106.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does the body depicted in this photograph correspond to the rectangular with the letters BJ that we saw in the earlier photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: BY, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Well, can we see the -- yeah. Okay. And what does this photograph depict then?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It shows the body of another male face down in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If this photograph could be -- before I tender this photograph, could we go back to the previous exhibit, which was tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The photograph that you saw a minute ago, is it still your understanding that body was lying at the position where you marked BY?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could go back to the photo of the body. Your Honours, I would seek to tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P243, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I have just three more. If we could see what is tab 12, a photograph from 65 ter number 201, the 21st photograph. ERN number N001-2110.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, did you take this photograph on the 14th of August?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what does it depict?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It depicts the body of another male, this time actually lying on his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P244, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could briefly look at tab 13, which is a photograph from 65 ter number 201, the 12th photograph in that series. It has ERN N000-2101.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: A third male, or a fifth one in these photographs, lying on his back, in the field further up from the body in the previous photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kind of wounds did you observe on this body?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Numerous, what I believe, to be gunshot exit wounds, on the front of the body, as you see there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P245, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, finally, Your Honours, if we could look at the photograph in tab 613 -- excuse me, tab 14 from 65 ter 613.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, it depicts a building that was burning at the time; and, in fact, not shown in this photograph, there are flames inside the building still. It was still burning, and on the asphalt road -- the photograph was taken deliberately to place these two things within the frame of it. On the right-hand side of the road, you see sort of a zigzag line. That is what I believe to be probably diesel oil fuel. The coincidence of placing them together seemed a little bit interesting at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P246, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And my apologies for going over time, at this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. We must now have our first morning break, and we resume at five minutes past 11.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon. Cross-examination by Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bolton. My name is Guenael Mettraux, and I appear, together with Edina Residovic, as counsel for Mr. Boskoski. Before we start, I would kindly ask you if you can pause after my questions before answering, and I will try to do the same after you have answered, so that we give a bit of time to the interpreters to catch up with us. I would like to take you immediately to the 10th of August, if I may, and I will summarize in a few lines some of the statement you have made in your first statement given to the Prosecution. I understand that on the 10th of August, that's Friday, around 8.00 or 8.30, you heard a loud explosion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you understood, from your military background and your familiarity with weapons and guns, that this sounded like a anti-tank mine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you tell me what time approximately you went or sought to go to Ljuboten after hearing that explosion?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do not recall the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can assist you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If the registry could bring up document 1D-112 with the ERN number of 1D00-1530. Your Honour, we also have court binders for Your Honours and for Mr. Bolton, which may be of an assistance, as there is a quite a great deal of documents which we'd like to deal with Mr. Bolton. So with the Court's assistance, we will distribute those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Bolton, when this document appears on your screen, you will get a data copy as well, which may be handier for you use, but those are the investigator's notes taken by Mr. Tucker of an interview which he had with you on the 25th of April 2002. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I remember meeting Mr. Tucker, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'll ask that you focus on the first page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And for Your Honours's benefit, this would be under tab 1 of the court binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As you will see, Mr. Bolton, the notes are being taken in the third form, with the "he" referring to you. Can I ask you to focus, first, on the third or fourth paragraph of that document, which starts with the word, "He stated that on Friday, 10th of August, 2001, he was working as a monitor for the OSCE." Can you see that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the next paragraph read as follows: "During the early afternoon of the 10th, exact time uncertain, he was with VC, Vladimir, Rogac, at the their accommodation in the village of Radisani." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would you think that the time which is indicated could be accurate?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I really don't recall exactly. I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you recall whether you sought go to Ljuboten in the afternoon of that day?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I sincerely cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You went to the village of Ljuboten from Radisani, is that correct, later that day?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: We tried to access Ljuboten in the area of the -- where we believe the explosion had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were you able to reach the outskirts of the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do not recall doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you see any check-points on the way, any police check-points on the way from Radisani towards Ljuboten on that day?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I recall that we tried to approach Ljuboten via Ljubanci, or we tried to approach Ljubanci, and we did not see any police check-points on the road to Ljubanci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is that correct, sir, that at the time there was no check-points, police check-points within the village of Radisani itself?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do not recall seeing any police check-points in Radisani that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you have just indicated that, on that day, you did not enter the village of Ljuboten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: No. I do not recall entering the village on that day. I'm -- it is simply a case of, now sitting here, which days we went in there and which we didn't. From this document, I cannot recall precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I may assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can ask the registry to turn to the next page of that document. That would be 1531 and -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to focus on the first paragraph of that document. It reads as follows: "Henry Bolton and Vladimir Rogac," I think it is a mistake; it should be VR, "attempted to obtain authorisation from the chain of command to go to Ljuboten to assess situation. They were refused permission to go to the village. The fire-fight eventually stopped." Would that be a correct record of what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Now I do not recall exactly, but I recall that we could not enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But from the position which you have managed to reach, I do understand that you were able to make a number of observation about what appeared to be going on in the village or around the village of Ljuboten; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I'm going to put a number of proposition, and I would kindly ask you to say whether you can agree with those? The first thing is you heard what you believe to be a heavy exchange of gun-fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you understood, as well, that this exchange of fire was not just a one-sided affair, but that there was, indeed, exchange between two sides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that was a position which was shared by your colleague, Mr. Rogac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you tell us for how long, approximately, you heard this fire going on?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: As I recall it now, it was some time. It was some extended period of time. It wasn't five minutes or so, it was a lot more than that, but I can't recall now exactly how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall until what time of day this activity continued?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, there's another documents which I would like to show you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That is Rule 65 ter 223. The ERN number is N001-5356, N001-5360.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, this is under the tab number 2 in your binder. Sir, am I correct to understand that this document is a special report issued by your organisation, the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is that correct that special reports of that sort or press releases which were distributed outside of the organisation would be vetted or would at least go through either the head of the mission or the deputy head of the mission?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I would not want -- this is not a press release. But, yes, special reports would be -- would be cleared through the reporting chain, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the time, sir, I think you have indicated the head of mission was Ambassador Ungaro?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And his deputy at the time was Robin Seward?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I think you have indicated to the Prosecutor in your proofing that your understanding was that Ms. Eileen Simpson might have been the author of that report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That is correct. That is my understanding. That is what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the time, Ms. Simpson was an UN dimension officer for the OSCE; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. Human dimension.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you just explain to us what procedure is followed when a special report of that sort is issued, in particular where it is being sent to?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, the normal procedure is that the author, who would generally be a manager, if you like, a head of a field station or a head of a department or a person with particular responsibilities, when they drafted the document, it would go to the next level of management for checking and clearance before going to the next and so on. Ultimately, the document, at the discretion of the head of mission, would be sent on to the OSCE Secretariat in Vienna or relative OSCE institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And once its been sent to Vienna, what happens with those documents? Are they then distributed to member states?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: They can be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is that also correct that reports such as those one, when particularly sensitive, may be kept confidential? They are not distributed to the public?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Going back to the 10th of August, sir, did you come to understand later or that day or later in time what had been happening north of the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you referring to the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what information did you obtain about that?
