utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I was concerned at the manner in which they appeared to have met their death, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps I will ask the registry once again to bring 1D24.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that is again, sir, the report of the 16th of August and it is at tab 2 of your document. That would be the second page of that document. And that would be the paragraph which starts with: "Two of the dead were along ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will read the paragraph to you: "Two of the dead were along or near the road where it passed through a residential area. Three others were found in a field on a hillside immediately above the uppermost house at the edge of town." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says this: "Based on observations of the scene, including the conditions of the bodies and the wounds they received, there is a particular concern regarding the circumstances of the deaths of the two men found within the town. Both of these individuals may have been shot at close range, and there are numerous spent shell casings in the area of the bodies." Is that consistent with your own observations, sir?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. With the -- the final sentence states: "Both of these individuals may have been shot at close range." I would emphasise "may" and that I wasn't the author of this report. There were certainly numerous spent shell casings in the area of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And your insistence, sir, on the word "may" is that you would not feel comfortable making any final determination on that point. Is that how I should understand it?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: My -- I'm confident that they were shot. I have no means to judge the distance from which they were shot or from which the bullets that hit them were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would that be correct, sir, that some of the injuries which you observed could also have been done post-mortem. Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Some, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will just move on to the next paragraph of the same report, sir. It starts with the word: "In the case of the first men, it was noted that there were what appeared to be gouge marks in the centre of a blood-stain on the pavement that were at least superficially consistent with the men having been shot whilst lying on the ground -- on the road," I'm sorry. Is that again at least consistent with your own observations?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, if we turn to the next page of that document at page 3. And, sir, that would be, again, the last paragraph but one, starting with the word "in any event." Is that correct, that the report goes on to sound a more cautious note when it says this: "It appears that the security forces moved up in this area in an action to clear it of any hostile forces that might be located there." And it says this: "It is also within the realm of possibility that the death of the first two men occurred during that operation." Would you agree, sir, that it would be a reasonable possibility, as indicated by your colleague in the report?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do not know what was in the mind of the author of this at the time, but -- and it also depends on the definition of the operation, but, yes, in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I think you have indicated, sir, in your own reports, or statement, I'm sorry, that did you not search any of the bodies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did not search them, I did not go through the pockets, I did not go -- did not search them for items on the body, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. If we turn now to the other three bodies that you observed which were further up the hills north of the village. If I may ask you to turn to the second page of this same document, and it is a paragraph that starts with the word "in contrast to the situation." That would be, I believe, the fourth paragraph. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In middle of that paragraph, it says this: "There is a general sense that their death," which is the three deceased, "are less suspicious and possibly related to legitimate military actions." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the report notes, in particular, that there were no shell casings around the bodies, which is consistent with your observation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There were also no superficial indications that they were shot at close range. Is that again consistent with your observations?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the report also notes that there were signs of fire on two -- to a nearby house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the report goes on to conclude that the men -- it appeared the men were shot from a distance while running uphill. Would that be again be consistent with your observations?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Generally, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would like to show you a picture, sir, which was taken by you on that day, and that is 1D129 under the ERN 1D001645, and that's under the tab number 23 in your binder. Can you recognise this picture, sir?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that would be the dead body of Mr. Xhelal Bajrami; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you would agree that Mr. Bajrami appears to be wearing what we could say are civilian clothes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you did not see any indication around him of any weapons or defensive position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I did not, yeah, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you understood this person to have been a civilian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: There was nothing to indicate otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's right. And, again, that's not a person that you searched. You have indicated that you didn't search any of the persons at the time.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would like to ask you whether you were later informed by Mr. Tucker or anyone else that 26 rounds of live ammunitions were found in the pockets of that person, or is that information that was not shared with you?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I certainly don't recall that information being shared with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And such information, sir, you would agree, would have been relevant to your assessment perhaps of the status of that person, had you had that information?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't see the -- oh, yes. I would like to tender this document, Your Honour, this picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D27, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, there's a few more pictures that I would like to show to you. The first one is a picture of Mr. Kadri Jashari, and it is at 1D130 under the ERN of 1D001646. Sir, I understand the picture is a black-and-white picture, so my question may be a bit unfair. But can you recall that this person was - it is tab 24 in your binder - that this person was bearing black trousers and a black jacket at the time of his death. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That is what I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn to the next picture which is under 1D131. That's a picture of Mr. Bajram Jashari, under 1D00-1647, and that's number 25, I would think. Well, sir, I should have used P41.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise to the Registry. I think we have a colour picture of this document, which is the same picture. P244, I am told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There again, sir, you would agree that Mr. Jashari was wearing black trousers and a black jacket; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Certainly dark, yes. Very close to black, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If we can go to the next picture, it would be 1D-132, 1D00-1648.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's under your tab 26, sir. That's a picture of Mr. Muharem Ramadan.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I understand it is also P186, although there may not be any markings of the name of the person on the Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But, sir, would you agree that, again, Mr. Ramadani, at the time, was wearing black trousers, a black shirt, and a black long coat?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Again, certainly dark, and I remember them as dark. Specifically black, I can't tell you. But certainly very dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you see, sir, on the chest of Mr. Ramadan, under the hole which you have identified, I believe, as an exit wound, can you see a black belt?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I can see something dark, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you observe that belt at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically. Certainly, my attention was not drawn to it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that at the time, one of the uniforms used by the NLA or combination of uniform was a black outfit, top to bottom?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, but not of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You would agree at least with me that a person in that sort of clothing could be mistaken then for a member of the NLA?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I cannot say that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you wonder, sir, why Mr. Ramadani was wearing a long, what would appear to be, leather black coat in the middle of the summer? Is that something that you asked yourself at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: No. It's common to come across Albanians in high temperatures, wearing what I would myself believe to be excessive amounts of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, sir, in the middle of the situation in the village, with an exchange of fire, would you agree with the possibility that that uniform could have been mistaken for that of a NLA or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe that, first of all, we've heard this before. We've heard this question asked and answered before; and second of all, the question as its formulated is really asking the witness to speculate, and I don't see how this will assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We'll proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, at the time, you were aware that the NLA would sometimes would wear a mixture of civilian and military clothes, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you would also agree with me that, at times, NLAs wearing uniforms would mingle with individuals wearing no uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I believe in every single case - and there were many that I had dealings with the NLA - they always wore something that would indicate that they were actually NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, could the Registry please bring back document 1D-123.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, sir, I'll ask to you look at the documents under tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Again, that is 1D19 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I will ask to you turn to the second page, please. And, again, this is, sir, the human rights developments report dated August 1st to 15th 2001, and the first paragraph say this: "As civilians and persons with little or no training become engaged in the conflict, the overall level of discipline in both forces can be expected to decline. Indeed, during the collapse of the cease-fire in Tetovo in August, armed ethnic Albanians in civilian clothes were observed moving through the city with groups of uniformed NLA." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you would agree that the OSCE, perhaps not you permanently, but some of your colleagues, have witnessed NLA in uniforms mingling around with people in -- identified as armed ethnic Albanians in civilian clothes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I cannot say that there were not such cases. I can refer to my own experience, which is that I believe in every case, there was something related to the dress of the individual that would indicate he was part of the group. The NLA often did -- they were part of community and they often did mingle with what I might term as non-combatants, but the combatants, those that considered themselves as combatants, invariably wore something to indicate the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, sir, that is your observation?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you receive information at the time, however, that members of the NLA in civilian clothes had been seen in the village at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Civilian clothes, yes -- well, at which time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, during the weekend in question, sir.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I have -- I may have received some information which I do not recall, but not from the monitors who were working with me, until we entered the village on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if we can go back, sir, to the second document in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, again, that is the special report of the 16th, and that is 1D24.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I ask you to turn to the third page of that document. And if we can go to the fourth paragraph which starts with the words, "There are several." And I would like to read to you the last sentence of your colleague who wrote the report, and he says this: "Reports from other international observers in the area indicate that there were EAAG in the village in civilian clothes and that there was an exchange of fire from deer rifles within the village." Am I right to understand that you personally did not possess that information at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: No. I did not, nor was I aware of any other international observers in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We're going to come back to that in a minute, sir. Another matter which I would like ask you about: Were you made aware at any stage of weapons being confiscated from within the village?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I do not recall of being informed of such a thing, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You've indicated, I think - and correct me if I'm wrong - but you have only visited or you have only gone inside one of the houses in the village on the 14th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I went into, I think, three or possibly four.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There's one I'm particularly interested in, and it is the basement in which you went and, I think, identified a gun and ammunition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you also understood at the time that this was the basement in which the first two person, whom you saw dead in Ljuboten, had been hiding earlier that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That is what I had been informed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you understood that those persons at the time had access to weapons.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Whilst they were in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have information at the time that hunting rifles had been used in the village during that incident, or did you only become aware of that information later on in time? I'm referring, again, to what I have just read to you.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There's another matter, sir, which I would like to --

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That weapon was not a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understood that you indicated that this weapon was or could be used for hunting birds; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Correct. But it is not a rifle. It was a shotgun and the -- the practical use of such a weapon compared to a rifle, which has a high velocity bullet, is very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I stand corrected on the type of weapon, sir. Thank you. There is another part of this report which I would like to discuss with you, and that is the next paragraph. But before that, is that correct, sir, that were not able to identify any of the persons who had killed any of the five persons whom you saw dead in the village on that day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, just to clarify, you're asking whether I could identify any individual --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Whether you had knowledge of the identity of any of the persons who might have killed those people.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: No. I did not have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention in relation to this issue on the next paragraph of the report of Ms. Simpson about this issue, and it says this: "It is possible there were exchanges between Macedonian villagers and Albanians villager, and also possible that there were Albanian to Albanian exchanges. It would be important to examine bodies to determine what kind of round caused their wounds. "It is possible that these persons were killed by army or by Macedonian villagers or by EAAG. The EAAG has recently lost two brigade commanders and is vigorously eliminating suspected moles and collaborators in the area under their control." Would you agree, sir, that, as suggested by your colleague and without a thorough examination of the bodies and a forensic examination, it would indeed be very, very difficult or impossible to determine who might have killed these people?

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: It's a judgement that I don't feel I'm able to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But it was not an unreasonable judgement on her part to make.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: I suppose not. I believe it is taken out of the context of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But, again, that is not an unreasonable conclusion to draw, the suggestion that the determination on that point should await further investigation, in particular, ballistic and forensic.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: That I would agree with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, sorry to interrupt. Would this be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely, your honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You were getting up steam again and getting up speed again, so I think we will let you relax. I'm sorry, Mr. Bolton, but we must adjourn to allow another Chamber to use the courtroom. So we resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps before we break, it has been drawn to my attention that the answer of Mr. Bolton was not recorded, and if Mr. Bolton could be kind enough to repeat his last answer for the record. My question was: It is not an unreasonable conclusion to draw the suggestion that a determination at that point should await further investigation, in particular forensic and ballistic? And I believe that you had you agreed with that proposition.

utterances.speaker: HENRY BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree that that would help determine the issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
